extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in cultural evolution, memetics, and internet culture
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the concepts, transmission mechanisms, and success/failure factors for memes (cultural units) both offline and online, and note theoretical/empirical critiques of memetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a meme
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea, behavior, or style that spreads by means of imitation (mimesis) from person to person within a culture and often carries symbolic meaning representing a particular phenomenon or theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include melodies, catchphrases, fashion, and the technology of building arches; in popular usage often refers to Internet memes (typically images) that are remixed, copied, and circulated online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meme as unit of cultural transmission (replicator properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: A meme acts as a unit for carrying cultural ideas, symbols, or practices that can be transmitted from one mind to another and is analogous to a gene in that it self-replicates, mutates, and responds to selective pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing emphasizes replication, mutation and selection as central properties to consider when evaluating whether something functions as a meme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dawkins' three conditions for evolution (applied to memes)
rubrics_metrics.description: For evolution to occur: (1) variation; (2) heredity or replication; and (3) differential 'fitness' (opportunity for one element to be more or less suited than another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memes must exhibit variation, be able to be copied/replicated, and have differential reproductive success to be treated as evolving entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention and transmission necessity (memetic lifecycle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes first need retention — the longer a meme stays in its hosts, the higher its chances of propagation — and they also need transmission (vertical or horizontal) to persist across time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threats to retention include reuse of neural space by other memes; retention without transmission is insufficient for long-term perpetuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of meme transmission (vertical/horizontal; imitation and communication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes reproduce by copying from a nervous system to another, either by communication or imitation; transmission can be vertical (parent to child) or horizontal (within a generation), and may be internal (i-memes) or external (e-memes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transmission vehicles include speech, writing, gestures, rituals, recorded media (books, musical scores), and internet platforms. Classification as i-meme vs e-meme highlights whether the meme is primarily internal mental content or mediated externally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aaron Lynch's quantity of parenthood
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea that influences the number of children one has; ideas that encourage higher birth rates will replicate at a higher rate vertically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a meme promotes behaviors that increase its vertical transmission through family lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aaron Lynch's efficiency of parenthood
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea that increases the proportion of children who will adopt the ideas of their parents (e.g., cultural separatism creating barriers to competing ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mechanisms that increase fidelity of parent-to-child cultural transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aaron Lynch's proselytic transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas passed to others beyond one's own children; proselytic memes spread horizontally and can replicate more rapidly across a generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a meme encourages active recruitment or evangelizing behaviors that expand its reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aaron Lynch's preservational transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas that influence those that hold them to continue to hold them for a long time, increasing the meme's longevity within hosts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for features that encourage durability (rituals, sanctions, narratives) making the meme resistant to replacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aaron Lynch's adversative transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas that influence those that hold them to attack or sabotage competing ideas and/or those who hold them; this aggressive protection can give transmission advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a meme includes adversarial elements (punishments for apostasy, demonization of rivals) that protect it from competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aaron Lynch's cognitive transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas perceived as cogent by most of the population who encounter them; these depend on pre-existing cognitive traits and spread passively rather than self-replicating strongly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how well a meme fits existing cognitive schemas and whether that fit aids passive spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aaron Lynch's motivational transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas people adopt because they perceive self-interest in adopting them; strictly speaking these don't self-propagate but often occur with other self-replicating modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish memes adopted for perceived personal benefit from those spreading via intrinsic replication dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes as discrete units — unitization problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty delimiting what constitutes a single meme: a meme can be a single word, a phrase, or an entire speech; there is no given size and the notion of discrete, indivisible meme 'units' is contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in treating cultural phenomena as atomic units; measurement and identification of units is a known theoretical challenge for memetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memeplexes and piggybacking (clusters of memes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clusters of memes (memeplexes) such as cultural or political doctrines replicate together and coadapt; memes fitting within a successful memeplex can gain acceptance by piggybacking on the memeplex's success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a meme's prospects, consider the larger memeplex it belongs to and whether it gains advantage from networked associations (example:religious doctrines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium as interactor — influence of meme vehicle
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium (meme-vehicle) influences the meme's evolutionary outcomes; some theorists argue the medium and idea are not distinct and that the medium affects copying fidelity and spread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the properties of the delivery medium (oral, written, audiovisual, internet) as they can enable or constrain replication and mutation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and psychological appeal increase spread (architectural memes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simpler memes with strong psychological appeal proliferate faster; architectural memes exemplify that 'the simpler they are, the faster they can proliferate' and that memes with great psychological appeal are most successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of antipatterns: visually striking but impractical architectural memes can spread despite being maladaptive; simplicity and mnemonic/prototypical appeal are engines of spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet meme features: remixability and deliberate alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet memes often are deliberately altered by human creativity (remixed) rather than mutating randomly; they spread rapidly via social networks, blogs, email, and news sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a meme's capacity to be remixed, parodied, or recontextualized and how internet affordances (sharing, virality mechanics) accelerate propagation (example: 'Gangnam Style' → 'Mitt Romney Style').

rubrics_metrics.name: Meme stocks: social-media-driven valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Meme stocks are companies lauded for the social media buzz they create rather than their operating performance; popularity on platforms can drive trading behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify 'meme stocks' by the degree to which their market movement is driven by online meme dynamics (subreddit coordination, viral interest) rather than fundamentals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darwinian vs Lamarckian traits in memetic evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Memetic evolution can show Darwinian (copying of instructions) and Lamarckian (copying of product/inference-driven) traits — e.g., learners may infer and reproduce skill outcomes rather than copying exact actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing transmission, note whether replication is high-fidelity copying (Darwinian) or inference-driven adaptation (Lamarckian), as this affects mutation and selection dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successful memes need not benefit hosts (parasitic memes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful meme may replicate effectively even when it is detrimental to the welfare of its hosts; memes that propagate less prolifically may become extinct regardless of host benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume host advantage is necessary for meme success; measure memes primarily by replication efficacy rather than host utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical grounding and measurability as evaluation criteria for memetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms of memetics point to lack of a 'code script' for memes, high mutation instability, and questions about whether memetics is a disprovable scientific theory; calls exist for empirical grounding (neuroimaging, population-analytic methods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess memetic claims against empirical measurability, testability, and interdisciplinary knowledge (sociology, anthropology, cognitive psychology); consider methods like neuroimaging or epidemiological analogues to measure memetic traces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semiotic and reductionist critiques (limits on explanatory power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Semiotic theorists argue memes are a degenerate concept of signs (copying only) and memetics can be reductionist compared to richer cultural theories; denying unitary meme status undermines the neo‑Darwinian analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using memetic analysis, account for translation, interpretation, and contextual semiotic processes rather than treating memes as simple replicators.
